subject: ice-floats
title: Why Ice Floats
summary: Ice is lighter for its size than water, and that keeps fish safe all winter.

keys.prompt: Why does an ice cube float in water?
keys.answer: Ice is less dense than liquid water. It packs less stuff into the same space, so it floats.

options.text: Ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is full of air from the freezer
Cold things always float

keys.prompt: What happens to water's tiny pieces when it freezes?
keys.answer: They line up in a neat pattern that holds them farther apart, so ice takes up more room.

options.text: They line up in a pattern with more space between them
They squeeze closer together
They stop being water

keys.prompt: How can fish live in a lake that has frozen over?
keys.answer: The ice floats on top like a lid. The water under it stays liquid, and the fish live there.

options.text: The ice floats on top and the water below stays liquid
Fish freeze and thaw out in spring
Lakes freeze from the bottom, so fish swim on top

cards.title: The cube that won't sink
cards.text: Drop an ice cube into a glass of water. It bobs right at the top. But for most stuff, the solid kind sinks in its own liquid. So what makes ice so different?

cards.question: How much of a floating ice cube sticks up above the water?

options.text: About one tenth
About half
Almost all of it

cards.reveal: About one tenth! Ice is about 90% as dense as water, so only about 10% of it pokes out above the top.

cards.title: Floating is about density
cards.text: Density means how much stuff is packed into a space. Things less dense than water float. Ice is only about 90% as dense as water. So about one tenth of an ice cube sits above the water.
cards.example: An iceberg works the same way. Most of it hides under the water.

cards.title: Ice is full of tiny gaps
cards.text: Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules. In liquid water they tumble around in a jumble. When water freezes, they lock into a neat pattern. That pattern holds them farther apart, so ice takes up more room.
cards.example: Fun fact: ice made from a rare kind called heavy water is denser than normal water. It sinks!

why.q: Why would a neat pattern take up more room than a jumble?
why.a: The pattern holds each molecule at a set distance from its neighbors. In a liquid they can crowd in closer.

cards.title: Lakes freeze from the top
cards.text: In winter, ice forms on top of a lake and stays there. It works like a lid between the cold air and the water below. The water under it stays liquid, so fish can live there all winter. If ice sank, a lake could freeze from the bottom up.

examples_by_interest.nature: Say you walk out on a frozen pond in January. Under the ice, the water is still liquid, and that is where the fish are.

cards.title: Freezing water pushes hard
cards.text: Water grows when it freezes, and it pushes with a lot of force. Water pipes can burst when the water in them freezes. Ice in cracks can even help break rocks apart.

cards.question: Imagine a world where ice sank. What would winter be like for fish, and for kids who like to skate?
nudges: Where would the ice end up in a lake?
Would there be ice on top to skate on?

options.text: It is less dense than liquid water
options.why: Yes. Ice packs less stuff into the same space.

options.text: It is colder than the water
options.why: Cold alone does not make things float. Density decides.

options.text: It has air bubbles inside
options.why: Some ice has air in it, but even clear ice floats. Its molecules are spaced out.

options.text: Its molecules lock into a pattern with gaps
options.why: Right. The gaps make ice take up more room.

options.text: Its molecules squeeze closer together
options.why: That happens for most things, but not for water.

options.text: It loses half its water
options.why: It is the same water. It just takes up more room.

questions.q: Why can fish live in a frozen lake?

options.text: The ice stays on top and the water below stays liquid
options.why: Yes. The floating ice is like a lid.

options.text: The fish freeze and wake up in spring
options.why: The fish live in the liquid water under the ice.

options.text: The ice sinks to the bottom
options.why: Ice floats, so it stays on top.

sources.title: Water Density
sources.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School
sources.supports: Density is mass per volume; ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice cubes float; in most substances the solid is denser; ice is about 90% as dense as water, so about 10% of an ice cube or iceberg sits above the water line; most of an iceberg is below the surface; ice molecules line up in a regular lattice that spreads them out more than in the liquid; if water were densest at freezing, lakes could freeze from the bottom up; 'heavy ice' from heavy water is denser than normal water and sinks.

sources.title: Ice
sources.supports: Because ice is less dense than liquid water it floats, which prevents bottom-up freezing and makes a sheltered place for life beneath it; ice expansion causes freeze-thaw weathering of rock; water pipes burst from the pressure of water expanding as it freezes.
